POSTMORTEM: Search latency incident, internal ticket OPS-4417

Summary
During the incident window the internal document search service returned p99 latencies above 14
seconds for 38 minutes, against a normal p99 of 240 milliseconds. Roughly 61 percent of search
requests in that window either timed out at the gateway or returned a partial result set. No data
was lost and no records were corrupted. The service recovered without a code rollback once the
originating configuration change was reverted.

Timeline
The change that triggered the incident was a routine tuning adjustment to the query result cache.
An engineer reduced the cache entry time to live from 600 seconds to 30 seconds, intending to make
freshly indexed documents visible sooner. The change was reviewed, approved and merged in the
normal way, and it shipped through the standard progressive rollout: one canary node, then twenty
five percent of the fleet, then the remainder.

The canary node showed no ill effects. Its cache hit rate fell from 94 percent to 71 percent, which
was expected and was in fact the point of the change, and its latency rose by about 18 milliseconds
at p99. The reviewer read that as an acceptable trade for fresher results. What the canary could
not show was the behaviour of the fleet as a whole, because the canary was carrying one thirty
second of the traffic and the cache is per node.

Eleven minutes after the change reached the full fleet, latency began to climb. Fourteen minutes
after that the first gateway timeouts appeared. The on call engineer was paged by the latency
alert, not by the error rate alert, because the error rate alert had a five minute evaluation
window and the timeouts were still being absorbed by client side retries.

Root cause
The service caches rendered result pages keyed by the normalised query string. With a 600 second
time to live, popular queries were served from cache almost continuously, and the underlying index
was queried only for the long tail. With a 30 second time to live, the most popular queries expired
twenty times more often. Each expiry allowed every concurrent request for that query to miss
simultaneously and issue its own index query, because the cache had no single flight protection. A
single popular query could therefore generate forty or fifty identical index reads in the same
second.

The index tier was sized for the steady state read volume, not for this multiplied volume. Its
thread pool saturated, queueing began, and queued index reads pushed the search tier past its own
connection pool limit. The two saturations reinforced each other. This is the classic cache
stampede, and the absence of single flight protection was the actual defect. The time to live
change merely exposed it.

Contributing factors
Three things made the incident longer than it needed to be. First, the canary stage could not
detect the failure mode by construction, since stampede severity scales with concurrent demand for
the same key and the canary had almost none. Second, the index tier had no queue depth metric
exported, so the first fifteen minutes of investigation were spent confirming a hypothesis that a
single dashboard panel would have answered. Third, the runbook for this service described how to
roll back a deployment but not how to revert a configuration value, and configuration was managed
by a separate system with a separate approval path.

Resolution
The engineer reverted the time to live to 600 seconds. Cache hit rates recovered within four
minutes and latency returned to baseline within seven.

Action items
Add single flight protection to the result cache so that only one request per key repopulates an
expired entry while the others wait. Export queue depth and thread pool saturation from the index
tier and add both to the service dashboard. Change the canary stage for cache related configuration
to a synthetic load stage that replays the top two hundred queries at production concurrency. Merge
the configuration revert procedure into the service runbook. Reduce the error rate alert evaluation
window from five minutes to ninety seconds. Finally, re attempt the freshness improvement, but do
it by invalidating cache entries on index write rather than by shortening the time to live.

Summarize the postmortem above in about 120 words for an engineering leadership audience. Cover the impact, the root cause, and the main follow-up actions.

PRODUCT SPECIFICATION: Unified Document Search, version 0.9 draft

Problem statement
Staff across four business units currently search for internal documents in five different places:
a wiki, a shared file store, a ticketing system, a contract repository and an archive of exported
message threads. Each has its own search box, its own relevance behaviour and its own permission
model. A survey of one hundred and twenty staff found that the median respondent checked three of
the five systems before giving up, and that thirty eight percent had at some point recreated a
document that already existed because they could not find it. The cost of that duplication is real
but hard to price; the cost in frustration is easy to observe.

Goal
Provide one search surface that returns results from all five sources, ranked together, while
respecting each source system as the authority on who may see what.

Non-goals
This is not a document management system. It does not become the place documents live, it does not
offer editing, and it does not attempt to deduplicate near identical documents across sources. It
also does not replace any source system's own search; those remain available and unchanged.

Users and their jobs
Three user types matter. The occasional searcher looks for a specific known document about once a
week and wants the right answer in the top three results. The researcher explores a topic, expects
to open eight or ten results, and needs filters by source, date and business unit. The
administrator needs to answer the question of why a particular person can or cannot see a
particular result, and needs it answered without reading code.

Functional requirements
Federated indexing. A connector per source pulls document text and metadata on a schedule and
writes to a single index. Connectors are independent; one failing connector degrades coverage for
its source only, and must surface that degradation in the interface rather than silently returning
fewer results.

Permission filtering at query time. The index stores an access control list per document, copied
from the source. Queries are filtered against the searcher's group membership before ranking.
Permission changes in a source system must be reflected within fifteen minutes. Filtering at query
time rather than at index time is deliberate: it costs latency but it avoids maintaining one index
per permission group.

Ranking. Combined lexical and semantic retrieval, with a single reranking pass. Recency is a
ranking signal weighted differently per source, because a contract from four years ago may be
entirely current while a wiki page from four years ago probably is not.

Filters and facets. Source, business unit, document type, last modified date range, and author
role. Facet counts must respect permission filtering, otherwise the counts themselves leak
information about documents the searcher cannot open.

Result presentation. Title, source badge, last modified date, a snippet with query terms
highlighted, and a direct link into the source system. No inline preview in the first release.

Non-functional requirements
Query latency at p95 under 800 milliseconds at the ninety fifth percentile index size. Availability
of 99.5 percent measured monthly. Index freshness of fifteen minutes for the wiki and ticketing
sources, and twenty four hours for the archive. The system must degrade to lexical only retrieval
if the semantic tier is unavailable, and must say so in the interface.

Open questions
Whether the archive of exported message threads should be in scope at all for the first release,
given that its permission model is the weakest of the five and would need to be reconstructed
rather than copied. Whether facet counts should be exact or approximate, since exact counts under
permission filtering are expensive. Whether the connector schedule should be push based, which is
faster and more complex, or pull based, which is slower and easier to reason about when a source is
down.

Success measures
Median number of systems checked per search task falls from three to one. Top three result accuracy
above seventy percent on a held out set of two hundred labelled queries. Weekly active searchers
above sixty percent of staff within one quarter of launch.

Summarize the product specification above in about 130 words. Cover the problem it solves, the two or three most important requirements, and the stated success measures.

MEETING NOTES: Quarterly capacity planning review, platform group

Attendees were the platform lead, two site reliability engineers, the data platform owner, the
finance business partner and a representative from the applications group. The meeting ran ninety
minutes. These notes are the record of decisions; the underlying spreadsheets are linked from the
planning workspace.

Context presented
Aggregate compute demand grew nineteen percent over the last quarter, against a forecast of twelve
percent. Two thirds of the overshoot came from a single workload, the nightly feature recomputation
job, which was expanded from a weekly cadence to a nightly cadence in the middle of the quarter
without a corresponding capacity request. The remaining third was ordinary organic growth spread
across roughly forty services.

Storage grew thirty one percent, which is closer to forecast than it sounds, because the forecast
assumed a retention policy change that was approved but never implemented. Without that change,
thirty one percent is the expected trajectory and will continue.

Discussion, compute
The site reliability engineers argued that headroom is now too thin. Peak utilisation on the shared
cluster reached eighty seven percent on four separate days, and the internal target is seventy
five. At eighty seven percent, a single node failure during peak causes visible queueing, and that
was observed twice. The applications representative countered that most of the peak is one
schedulable batch job and that moving it would be cheaper than buying capacity.

The data platform owner accepted that the nightly job could move to a window between 02:00 and
05:00 local, but noted a hard dependency: the job consumes a snapshot produced by an upstream
extract that currently finishes at 01:10 and has itself been slipping later. Moving the job without
first stabilising the upstream extract would simply relocate the problem.

Decision one: the nightly feature recomputation job moves to the 02:00 window, effective after the
upstream extract has been stabilised. The data platform owner owns the stabilisation work and will
report a completion date within two weeks. No capacity is purchased for this workload in this
quarter.

Discussion, storage
Finance noted that storage is now the fastest growing line item and is on track to overtake compute
within three quarters if the trajectory holds. The retention policy change that was approved last
quarter would remove roughly eighteen percent of current volume, mostly intermediate artefacts from
completed pipeline runs older than ninety days. It was not implemented because no one owned it.

There was a discussion about whether the intermediate artefacts have any value after ninety days.
The data platform owner said they are occasionally used to reproduce a historical result during an
audit, perhaps twice a year, and that regenerating them costs roughly six hours of compute each
time. The consensus was that six hours of compute twice a year is obviously cheaper than storing
everything for a year, and that the policy should proceed.

Decision two: the ninety day retention policy is implemented this quarter. The platform lead owns
it. A dry run listing what would be deleted is circulated for objections before anything is
removed, and the deletion is staged over four weeks rather than done at once.

Discussion, forecasting
Everyone agreed the forecast missed because a workload cadence change bypassed capacity review.
There is no gate today; the change was legitimate and correctly reviewed for correctness, but no
one asked what it would cost to run.

Decision three: any change that alters a scheduled workload's cadence, concurrency or data volume
by more than a factor of two requires a capacity note in the review. The note is two lines and an
estimate, not a formal process. The platform lead drafts the template.

Follow ups
Upstream extract stabilisation date, within two weeks, data platform owner. Retention dry run,
within three weeks, platform lead. Capacity note template, within one week, platform lead. Revised
forecast incorporating all three decisions, before the next review, finance business partner.

Summarize the meeting notes above in about 120 words. State each decision that was made and who owns the follow-up.

RELEASE NOTES: Data pipeline platform, version 4.2

This release focuses on scheduler correctness, backfill ergonomics and connector stability. It is
a minor version, but it contains two behaviour changes that require operator attention before
upgrading. Read the upgrade notes at the end before deploying to a production environment.

New features

Partitioned backfills. A backfill can now be declared over a partition range rather than a wall
clock range, and the scheduler will expand the range into one task per partition. Previously an
operator had to submit each partition separately or write a wrapper script. Partition expansion
respects the pipeline's declared maximum parallelism, so a thousand partition backfill no longer
saturates the worker pool. Progress is reported per partition and a failed partition can be retried
without resubmitting the whole range.

Connector health surface. Every source connector now exports a structured health record containing
last successful poll, last error, consecutive failure count and estimated lag. The scheduler reads
these records and refuses to start a downstream task whose upstream connector has been failing for
longer than a configurable threshold, defaulting to thirty minutes. This replaces the previous
behaviour, where a downstream task would start, read a stale partition and succeed with wrong data.

Dry run mode for transformations. A transformation can be executed against a sampled subset of its
input with all writes redirected to a scratch namespace. The output schema and row count are
reported and nothing durable is written. This is intended for reviewing a transformation change
before merging it.

Improvements

Task scheduling latency at the ninety fifth percentile is reduced from about nine seconds to about
two, mostly by replacing a polling loop in the dispatcher with a notification channel. Log lines
from workers now carry the pipeline name, task identifier and attempt number as structured fields
rather than as free text, which makes them queryable. The command line client gained a status
subcommand that summarises a pipeline's last twenty runs in one screen. Memory use in the metadata
service is reduced by roughly a third under wide pipelines, by streaming task listings rather than
materialising them.

Bug fixes

A retry storm could occur when a task failed during its own cleanup phase, because the cleanup
failure was recorded as a task failure and the task was rescheduled with its side effects already
partially applied. Cleanup failures are now recorded separately and do not trigger a retry. A
timezone handling error caused schedules expressed in a zone with a half hour offset to fire thirty
minutes late on the day of a daylight saving transition. Task logs longer than sixteen megabytes
were silently truncated in the middle rather than at a line boundary, producing invalid records at
the tail. Two connectors leaked file handles when a source returned an empty response body.

Behaviour changes requiring attention

First, the connector health gate described above is enabled by default. Pipelines that previously
ran on stale data and appeared healthy will now block instead. This is the correct behaviour, but
it will surface as new failures on upgrade day for anyone with a chronically failing connector.
Review connector health before upgrading and either fix the connector or raise the threshold
explicitly.

Second, task retries no longer inherit the original submission's priority. A retried task is queued
at the default priority for its pipeline. Deployments that relied on high priority tasks retaining
priority across retries should set the priority at the pipeline level instead of per submission.

Deprecations

The legacy cron expression parser is deprecated and will be removed in version 5.0. It differs from
the standard parser in its handling of the day of month and day of week fields when both are
specified. Run the supplied migration checker to see which schedules are affected.

Upgrade notes
Upgrade the metadata service first, then the scheduler, then the workers. The metadata schema
migration is forward compatible with the previous scheduler, so a partial upgrade is safe. Rolling
back the metadata migration is not supported; take a backup first.

Summarize the release notes above in about 130 words for an operator who has to decide when to upgrade. Prioritise the behaviour changes that require attention.

POSTMORTEM: Write loss during an unplanned database failover, internal ticket OPS-4602

Impact
Over a window of six minutes and forty seconds, the order intake service accepted and acknowledged
1,412 write operations of which 87 were not present after the failover completed. Those 87 writes
were acknowledged to callers as durable. Nine of them were reconstructed from an upstream message
log; the remaining 78 were reconstructed from application side idempotency records after the
affected teams were contacted. No write was permanently lost, but the system asserted durability it
did not have, and that is the finding.

What happened
The primary database instance became unresponsive to health checks. The managed failover controller
observed three consecutive failed health checks over fifteen seconds and promoted the standby
replica. Promotion took roughly forty seconds, during which the intake service saw connection
errors and retried. After promotion, the service reconnected to the new primary and resumed
serving. Ordinary monitoring showed a short error spike and then recovery, and no one looked
further for two days.

The gap surfaced when a reconciliation job comparing the intake service's own request log against
database contents reported a mismatch. That job runs weekly and exists for exactly this reason.

Root cause
Replication between primary and standby was configured as asynchronous. This was a deliberate
choice made two years earlier to reduce write latency, and it was documented in the database
configuration repository. What was not carried forward into the service's own durability claims was
what asynchronous replication means during an unplanned promotion: any write acknowledged by the
primary but not yet shipped to the standby is lost when the standby is promoted.

Under normal load the replication lag was under fifty milliseconds and the exposure would have been
a handful of writes. On the day of the incident the primary had been under unusual write pressure
from an unrelated bulk import, and measured replication lag had been between two and four seconds
for about twenty minutes before the health checks failed. The lag was visible on a dashboard. It
was not alerted on.

Why the failure was invisible
The intake service returns success to its caller when the database driver returns success. The
driver returns success when the primary acknowledges. Nothing in that chain has any knowledge of
whether the write reached the standby, so there is no signal the service could have used to know it
was at risk. The service's public contract said writes are durable once acknowledged. That
contract was written against a synchronous replication assumption that had been changed underneath
it without the contract being revisited.

Contributing factors
Replication lag had no alert. The failover controller had no minimum lag precondition and would
promote a standby that was arbitrarily far behind, on the theory that an available stale database
beats an unavailable current one. That theory is defensible for a read heavy service and wrong for
this one. Finally, the reconciliation job that found the problem runs weekly, so the detection
delay was up to seven days by design.

Resolution
Not applicable in the usual sense; the failover itself succeeded and the database was healthy
throughout the investigation. The remediation is the action list.

Actions
Alert on replication lag above five hundred milliseconds sustained for one minute, paging during
business hours and ticketing otherwise. Configure the failover controller to prefer a standby whose
lag is under a threshold, and to require an explicit human decision when no standby qualifies.
Change the intake service to record a durable request log entry before calling the database, so
reconstruction is mechanical rather than a manual exercise. Rewrite the service's durability
contract to state what is actually guaranteed. Increase the reconciliation job frequency from
weekly to hourly. Review every other service sharing this database topology for the same
mismatched durability claim; there are four, and two of them make the same claim.

Summarize the postmortem above in about 120 words. Be explicit about what was lost, why it was lost, and what will prevent a recurrence.

PRODUCT SPECIFICATION: Field Inspection Companion, offline first mobile application, draft 3

Background
Field inspectors visit sites to record equipment condition. Roughly forty percent of the sites have
no usable mobile data connection, and a further twenty percent have a connection so intermittent
that a request may take minutes to complete or may fail after appearing to succeed. The current
tool is a web form. Inspectors work around it by photographing equipment, writing on paper, and
retyping everything in the evening. Retyping is where the errors come from, and it is where roughly
seventy minutes per inspector per day goes.

Goal
An application in which the inspector's work is complete when they leave the site, regardless of
connectivity, and in which synchronisation is a background concern the inspector never has to
think about.

Core principle
The device is the source of truth for work in progress. The server is the source of truth for
completed and accepted inspections. Nothing the inspector does on site requires a network call, and
no inspection is ever blocked by a failed synchronisation.

Functional requirements

Local first data model. The full inspection schedule for the next fourteen days, the equipment
register for every scheduled site, and the current checklist templates are downloaded when the
device has connectivity and stored locally. The inspector can open any scheduled inspection with
the device in airplane mode and complete it end to end.

Capture. Structured checklist responses, free text notes, photographs and short audio notes.
Photographs are compressed on device to a target size and the original is retained until
synchronisation succeeds, then discarded. Audio notes are stored and uploaded but are not
transcribed in the first release.

Deterministic synchronisation. Each locally created record carries a client generated identifier
and a monotonically increasing local sequence number. Uploads are idempotent on that identifier, so
a retry after an ambiguous failure cannot create a duplicate. The synchronisation engine uploads in
sequence order and stops on the first unrecoverable error rather than skipping ahead, so partial
state is always a prefix of the inspector's work rather than an arbitrary subset.

Conflict handling. Conflicts are rare by construction because an inspection is owned by one
inspector, but they occur when a scheduler reassigns a site while an inspection is in progress. The
rule is that the inspector's completed record always wins and the reassignment is rejected with a
notification to the scheduler. Silent data loss on the device is never acceptable, even when the
device is wrong.

Visible synchronisation state. A single persistent indicator shows one of four states: everything
uploaded, uploads pending with a count, upload blocked with a reason, and offline. The inspector
should never have to guess.

Non-functional requirements
Cold start to a usable inspection screen in under three seconds on the oldest supported device
class. Local storage budget of four gigabytes, with automatic pruning of accepted inspections older
than thirty days. Battery cost of a full working day of capture below twenty five percent on the
reference device. All local data encrypted at rest, with the key protected by the device credential.

Out of scope for the first release
Multi inspector collaboration on a single inspection, offline map tiles, transcription of audio
notes, and any form of real time supervisor visibility into an inspection that has not been
submitted.

Risks
The largest risk is storage growth from photographs on devices that stay offline for a week or
more; the pruning rule does not help because nothing is accepted yet. The mitigation is a hard cap
with an explicit warning at eighty percent. The second risk is that a schema change to a checklist
template invalidates work already captured offline; templates are therefore versioned and a device
completes an inspection using the template version it downloaded.

Summarize the product specification above in about 130 words. Cover the core principle, the synchronisation design, and what is out of scope.

MEETING NOTES: API versioning decision, integration working group

Purpose of the meeting was to decide how the public integration API handles breaking changes, and
to stop the current practice of deciding case by case. Present were the API owner, two service
team leads, the developer relations lead, the support lead and a technical writer.

The problem as stated
There have been three breaking changes in eighteen months and each was handled differently. The
first added a required field and was shipped with a two week notice on a status page; it broke
eleven integrations and generated forty support tickets. The second renamed a field and was shipped
behind a header opt in, which worked well but nobody documented the header, so adoption was near
zero and the old behaviour is still being maintained. The third removed an endpoint after a six
month deprecation window and went almost unnoticed, which everyone agreed was the only good outcome
of the three.

Support reported that the recurring theme in tickets is not the change itself but the surprise.
Integrators are generally willing to do work; they are not willing to discover at two in the
morning that they need to.

Options considered
Option one, URL path versioning, with a version segment in the path and a new version for any
breaking change. Familiar to integrators, trivially visible in logs, and easy to route. The
objection is that it encourages coarse versioning: a single field rename forces a whole new surface
and integrators must migrate everything at once even if only one endpoint changed.

Option two, header based versioning with a date value, where a client pins a date and the server
serves the behaviour as of that date. Fine grained, allows a client to move forward gradually, and
keeps one URL surface. The objection is that it is invisible in ordinary logs and in a browser
address bar, and that the server must maintain a transformation chain, which grows without bound
unless old dates are retired.

Option three, no versioning and additive only changes forever. Rejected quickly; the group agreed
it is not honest, because sooner or later a field's meaning has to change and pretending otherwise
just produces a field named the same thing that means something new.

Decision
Header based date versioning, with the following constraints agreed in the room. A client that
sends no version header is pinned to the date of its first observed request and is told so in a
response header. Every response carries the resolved version date, so the value is visible in
integrator logs even though the request may not carry it. Versions older than eighteen months may
be retired, with a six month notice, and the notice is sent to the technical contact on the
integration record and not only posted on a status page. The transformation chain is capped at
twelve live versions; if the cap is reached, retiring the oldest becomes a blocking prerequisite for
adding a new one.

Additive changes do not create a version. The definition of additive is fixed as: adding an optional
request field, adding a response field, adding a new endpoint, or adding a new enumerated value to a
field explicitly documented as open ended. Everything else is breaking.

Actions
The API owner writes the versioning policy document. The technical writer produces the integrator
facing migration guide template, so that every future version ships with one. Developer relations
drafts the notification mechanism, including how technical contacts are kept current, and reports
back on whether contact data is good enough to rely on. The support lead defines the two metrics the
group will judge this by: tickets per version transition, and the fraction of integrations still on
a version older than twelve months. Review in one quarter.

Summarize the meeting notes above in about 120 words. State the decision reached, the main reason the alternatives were rejected, and the agreed follow-up actions.

RELEASE NOTES: Observability agent, version 2.0

Version 2.0 is a major release. The agent has been restructured around a single pipeline model,
several long standing configuration keys have been removed, and the on disk buffer format has
changed. Plan the upgrade rather than rolling it out automatically.

What changed structurally
Previous versions ran three semi independent collectors for metrics, logs and traces, each with its
own configuration file, its own buffer and its own exporter. Behaviour differed between them in ways
that were never intentional: only the log collector retried on export failure, only the metric
collector applied resource attributes, and only the trace collector respected the proxy setting. In
2.0 all three feed one pipeline with one buffer, one exporter and one retry policy. Consistency is
the point of the release.

New capabilities

Unified resource attributes. Host, environment, service and custom attributes are declared once and
applied to every signal. Previously the same attribute had to be declared in up to three places and
frequently drifted between them.

Adaptive sampling for traces. The agent can hold a configurable trace budget per minute and prefer
traces that contain an error or exceed a latency threshold. Head based sampling at a fixed rate
remains available and is still the default, because adaptive sampling changes what the data means
and should be an explicit choice.

Disk buffer with bounded growth. The buffer is a segmented file with a hard size cap and an explicit
policy when the cap is reached: drop oldest, drop newest, or block the collector. The previous
behaviour was to grow until the filesystem filled, which on two occasions took down the host the
agent was supposed to be observing.

Configuration validation. The agent validates its full configuration at startup and refuses to start
on an invalid file, printing every error rather than the first. Previously an unrecognised key was
ignored silently, which meant a typo in a key name disabled a feature without any signal.

Removals and breaking changes

The three separate configuration files are replaced by one. A conversion tool is supplied and
handles the great majority of configurations mechanically; it reports anything it cannot convert
rather than guessing.

The keys named for the old per collector retry, proxy and attribute settings are removed rather than
deprecated, because their semantics differed per collector and silently mapping them to the unified
equivalents would change behaviour without telling anyone. The conversion tool maps them and prints
what it did.

The on disk buffer format has changed and is not readable by the previous version. Data buffered by
version 1.x is not migrated; drain the buffer before upgrading, or accept the loss of whatever was
pending. The upgrade procedure below drains it.

Minimum supported host requirements have risen. The agent now requires a 64 bit host and a kernel
with the newer filesystem notification interface.

Performance
Resident memory on a typical host falls from about 210 megabytes to about 140, because one buffer
replaces three. Export throughput improves by roughly forty percent under back pressure, mostly from
batching across signal types. Startup time increases by about half a second because of configuration
validation, which is considered a fair trade.

Upgrade procedure
Run the conversion tool against the existing configuration files and review its report. Stop the
agent with the drain flag and wait for the buffer to empty; the drain reports remaining segments
every ten seconds. Install version 2.0. Start it with the validate only flag and confirm a clean
result. Start the agent normally. Confirm that all three signal types are arriving before moving to
the next host group. Roll forward one host group at a time; there is no supported downgrade once the
new buffer format has been written.

Summarize the release notes above in about 130 words. Emphasise the breaking changes and the required upgrade procedure.
